lesson.title: Running Totals: Turning a Rate Into a Quantity
lesson.summary: An accumulation function F(x) equal to the integral from a to x of f(t) dt takes a rate, such as velocity or flow, and produces the running total quantity it has produced by time x, with FTC part one guaranteeing that F'(x) is exactly that rate again.
lesson.body:
Many quantities in the real world are naturally described as rates: velocity is the rate at which position changes, a flow rate is the rate at which volume fills a tank, marginal cost is the rate at which total cost grows with each additional unit produced. Whenever you have a rate f(t) and you want to know the total amount accumulated between a starting time a and some later time x, the accumulation function F(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt is exactly the tool for the job. It is precisely the same object introduced in FTC part one, just viewed through the lens of a concrete running total rather than an abstract area.

Notice again the deliberate choice of letters: the rate is written as a function of t, the dummy variable being swept across the interval of accumulation, while x is the input to F that decides where the running total is being read off. Reusing x for both roles would be genuinely ambiguous, since one x needs to vary continuously as the accumulation sweeps forward while the other x needs to sit still as the point where you stop and check the total. Keeping them as separate letters, t inside the integral and x outside it, avoids that confusion entirely.

Here is a worked example. Suppose an object moves with velocity v(t) = 4 - t, measured in units per second, starting from position 0 at time t = 0. The accumulated position at time x is s(x) = the integral from 0 to x of v(t) dt. An antiderivative of 4 - t is 4t - t^2/2, so s(x) = 4x - x^2/2. At x = 3, s(3) = 4 times 3 - 9/2 = 12 - 4.5 = 7.5. Since v(t) = 4 - t stays positive for every t between 0 and 3 (it only reaches 0 at t = 4), the object never reverses direction during this interval, so the accumulated position 7.5 also equals the total distance traveled, not just the net displacement.

This example is FTC part one wearing a physical costume. Differentiating the position function gives s'(x) = 4 - x, which is exactly v(x), the velocity the whole construction started from. That is not a coincidence, it is the same statement as F'(x) = f(x) from the fundamental theorem, just phrased in the language of motion: the derivative of accumulated position is velocity, because velocity is, by definition, the rate at which position accumulates.
